Red Sox Year in Review 2026: Looking Back at Payton Tolle's Season originally appeared on NESN. Add NESN as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Arguably no individual player captured the Red Sox's turnaround to make the postseason in 2026 more than Payton Tolle.
Coming into the season, as a former second-round pick who started the year in Triple-A, Boston didn't have much higher expectations than Tolle becoming a potential back-end rotation pitcher, with a chance he could be moved to the bullpen if necessary. With bigger names like Sonny Gray, Garrett Crochet, Brayan Bello and Ranger Suarez leading the way, there wasn't a lot of room for Tolle to prove himself.
But Tolle wound up surpassing even the most modest expectations. He didn't just break out in the wake of Crochet's long-term injury — he immediately became one of the best pitchers in the American League.
Here's a look back at Tolle's remarkable 2026 season, becoming a fan favorite with the Red Sox.
Red Sox Year in Review 2026: Payton Tolle
Tolle didn't come completely out of nowhere in 2026. As a former TCU star who was named the Big 12 Pitcher of the Year in 2024, he landed with the Red Sox as a second-round pick in the 2024 MLB Draft. Just how quickly he was MLB-ready, though, was a pleasant surprise.
After reaching Triple-A by August 2025, Tolle was called up to the Red Sox last September, making a few starts late in the regular season before making the team's AL Wild Card roster as a bullpen option. To open 2026, Tolle was considered a top pitching depth option for Boston, starting the season in Triple-A to continue developing a bit before he got another MLB shot.
It didn't take long. By the end of April, with the Red Sox off to a poor start and Crochet ruled out with an injury soon after, Tolle was called up on Apr. 23 to pitch against the Yankees.
He made quite the first impression, striking out 11 in six innings of work.
From there, Tolle's spot in the rotation was secured, and he became one of Chad Tracy's top trusted arms on what became a strong Red Sox pitching staff. Tolle carried a sub-3.00 ERA into June and was a reliable arm to go at least five innings on a nightly basis — he out-performed virtually all expectations by becoming one of the best left-handed pitchers in baseball.
By the time the Red Sox had turned their season around, Tolle was a significant reason, and he earned the trust of Tracy to pitch in Game 1 of the AL Wild Card series.
Still just 23 years old, Tolle is now in place to remain one of Boston's top arms for years to come. With his jolly personality, he also quickly became a fan favorite, always a candidate to have the most wholesome moment of the night or crack a joke.
Payton Tolle's most memorable moment
There's a lot to choose from here — Tolle struck out 11 Yankees in his first start of the season after beginning the year in Triple-A, went seven scoreless innings against the Tigers in May and the Yankees in June, became the youngest Red Sox pitcher to reach 14 strikeouts in a game since Roger Clemens, and pitched for Boston in the AL Wild Card series after becoming a trusted arm.
However, considering Tolle pulled off a feat that only so many pitchers accomplish, it's hard not to go with his immaculate inning on Sept. 13.
Towards the end of the regular season, Tolle took the mound against the Royals, and he needed nine pitches to strike out three Kansas City batters. And he certainly had fun doing it.
By the time he was eight pitches in, Tolle knew he needed one more strike to accomplish the feat against Jac Caglianone, cracking a smile before he fired a pitch past the Royals slugger and pumped his fist.
This is genuinely one of the most amazing things I’ve ever watched in a baseball game. Not just throwing an immaculate inning, but also knowing it, smiling at it, and laughing after he did it. Payton Tolle can’t be real, man. https://t.co/kUjZ0lp0n1
— Robbie Hyde (@gingersnaphyde) September 13, 2026
Tolle became the first Red Sox pitcher to record an immaculate inning since Chris Sale in 2021 and the first to accomplish the feat in the first inning since Pedro Martinez in 2002.
Whether with his arm, or just his goofy personality, Tolle was full of memorable moments in his first full MLB season.
Payton Tolle stats for 2026 season
| Starts | IP | ERA | WHIP | K | BB | K/9 | bWAR | fWAR |
| 26 | 148.2 | 3.03 | 1.29 | 171 | 40 | 10.4 | 2.9 | 4.1 |
Tolle certainly looks like the kind of arm who can take a more significant workload in years to come. At 6-foot-6, 250 pounds, he totaled 148.2 innings in his first MLB season, one of the top strikeout artists in MLB. Had he qualified in innings, Tolle would have had a K/9 comparable to Paul Skenes (10.3) and Cristopher Sanchez (10.0).
Boston didn't push Tolle too hard, though, often facing a leash around 90 pitches. As he spend more time in the big leagues, it wouldn't be surprising to see him become a workhorse.
For now, 148 innings' worth of excellence was more than enough from Tolle, becoming a significant piece of the Red Sox's future.

item.content:encoded:
This year's World Series will have a tough act to follow. Not only was the 2025 World Series between the Los Angeles Dodgers and Toronto Blue Jays the first seven-game affair since 2019, but it featured an 18-inning game and then a Game 7 that might have been the greatest baseball game ever played.
The good news is we're guaranteed that a long-starved fanbase will get to celebrate in 2026. The Milwaukee Brewers, coming off their impressive and dynamic four-game sweep of the Dodgers in the NLCS, are in the Fall Classic for the first time since 1982 and seek the first championship in franchise history, looking to put an exclamation point on their season after leading the majors with 103 wins.
The Tampa Bay Rays were a 1998 expansion franchise and reached the World Series in 2008 and 2020 (the shortened season during the COVID-19 pandemic) but are seeking their first title as well. Young power hitter Junior Caminero and unheralded staff ace Drew Rasmussen lead the way as the Rays look to finally cash in after making the playoffs six times in the past eight seasons.
The Brewers and Rays led their respective leagues in wins, always a bonus for those who want the best teams in the World Series. Of course, a lot of attention will be given to the small-market aspect of the matchup, as the cloud of the lockout looms in the offseason.
Let's rank all the World Series since 2000 to see where Brewers-Rays fits in. This ranking is based on hype, the quality of the teams and their star power heading into the World Series. It's not a ranking of the quality of the World Series itself, although we're going to include a grade on that for each matchup. Let's get to it.
The Yankees were back in the World Series for the sixth time in eight years, and the Marlins had rebuilt after their fire sale following their World Series title in 1997. Trust me when I say that nobody wanted the Yankees in the World Series yet again. And the Marlins were merely a 91-win wild-card team. Most notably, however, both teams had spoiled the ultimate World Series by knocking off the Cubs and Red Sox -- before either team had overcome its curse -- in Game 7s in the LCS.
Actual World Series: C. The Marlins won Game 4 in 12 innings, when Yankees manager Joe Torre inexplicably failed to use reliever Mariano Rivera, and then 23-year-old Josh Beckett tossed a five-hit shutout in Game 6.
In an all-wild-card series, the fifth-seeded Rangers had won 90 games and the sixth-seeded Diamondbacks won only 84, making this the lowest combined win total in World Series history (for full seasons). The Rangers were going for their first World Series title, so there was that, and there were some fun hitters -- Corey Seager, the red-hot Adolis Garcia (who had just driven in 15 runs in the ALCS) and Corbin Carroll -- but it was a soft matchup on paper.
Actual World Series: D-. The series turned on Seager's tying two-run homer off Paul Sewald in the bottom of the ninth of Game 1, which Garcia then won with a home run in the 11th. There wasn't a single lead change after that, and three of those games were blowouts.
This was the Cardinals team that got hot in September and clinched a wild-card spot on the final day of the season when the Braves blew a lead in the ninth inning and lost in extra innings. St. Louis certainly had star power with the likes of Albert Pujols, Lance Berkman and Matt Holliday but had won a World Series fairly recently (2006), and the Rangers had just been there the year before.
Actual World Series: A. The first two games were one-run games, including the Rangers pulling out a victory with two runs in the ninth. In Game 3, Pujols blasted a record-tying three home runs. Game 6 was the David Freese Game -- perhaps the single most exciting baseball game ever played. Game 7 was a bit of an anticlimactic 6-2 Cardinals win.
The second-lowest combined win total in World Series history featured two wild-card teams that won fewer than 90 games. The Royals were at least a good story -- in the playoffs for the first time since winning the World Series in 1985 -- and had gone 8-0 in the AL playoffs, including an epic win over the A's in the wild-card game. The Giants, however, had just won the World Series in 2010 and 2012, and this team didn't seem nearly as good as those two.
Actual World Series: B-. Five of the games were blowouts, but it did at least go seven. It'll be remembered for Madison Bumgarner's historic performance: a shutout in Game 5 (the last complete game shutout in World Series history) and then five scoreless innings of relief in Game 7, getting Salvador Perez to pop out with the tying run on third to end it.
The Red Sox were only three years removed from breaking the Curse of the Bambino in 2004, so although they were still a star-laden team with David Ortiz, Manny Ramirez and scrappy rookie Dustin Pedroia, they were no longer as interesting. The Rockies were a fun story, winning 14 of their final 15 games, including beating the Padres in a tiebreaker, just to win a wild-card spot. Then they went 7-0 in the NL playoffs and had won 21 of 22 entering the World Series.
Actual World Series: F.A dud. Two of the games were one-run games, but this goes down as one of the least memorable World Series of all time, with a forgettable four-game sweep.
The Tigers were the story of the season. They had lost 119 games three years before and 91 just the previous year. With rookie starter Justin Verlander winning 17 games, they led the AL Central most of the season -- only to lose their final five games and squeak into the playoffs as a wild-card team. The Cardinals won a weak NL Central with only 83 wins -- although they at least had Pujols at his absolute peak (.331/.431/.671, 49 home runs). Both teams hadn't won a World Series in a couple of decades: 1982 for the Cardinals, 1984 for the Tigers. Plus, it did feature two of the original 16 franchises.
Actual World Series: F. The Cardinals won one game in the bottom of the eighth, but it was otherwise a blur of nothing, most characterized by several fielding miscues by Tigers pitchers. David Eckstein won MVP honors without hitting a home run and while driving in only four runs.
The Braves were back in the World Series for the first time since 1999 -- they had made 12 playoff appearances in the intervening years without making it to the Fall Classic. Still, this was the weakest of the Atlanta playoff teams of recent vintage, winning only 88 games and missing Ronald Acuña Jr. for the playoffs. The Astros, meanwhile, were back in the World Series for the third time in five years -- but the first time since the 2017 sign-stealing scandal had broken in November 2019. Let's just say not everyone wanted them there.
Actual World Series: D. This was a weird World Series. The Braves ended up going with two bullpen games (who remembers that Dylan Lee and Tucker Davidson started?) after Charlie Morton broke a leg in Game 1. Astros starters kept getting knocked out early (the only starter to go more than five innings for either team was Max Fried in the finale). Four of the games were blowouts.
The Giants were back after winning in 2010, and the Tigers were back for the first time since 2006, featuring Triple Crown winner Miguel Cabrera and a strong 1-2 punch in the rotation with Verlander and Max Scherzer. This was also the last World Series with that season's MVP winners until Aaron Judge and Shohei Ohtani in 2024, with Cabrera and Buster Posey.
Actual World Series: D-. A boring sweep. Pablo Sandoval did hit three home runs in Game 1, but there were two shutouts and chilly weather in Detroit made the final two games unbearable.
This one did feature the two best teams from the regular season (both won 97 games), the last time before this year that we had that happen in a full season. It was also a classic original-16 matchup, although we had seen this in 2004 -- plus, both teams had won recently (2007 for Boston, 2011 for St. Louis). These were veteran teams, with Ortiz leading the Red Sox and the Cardinals featuring four .300 hitters, plus Carlos Beltran, who hit .296 and led the team in home runs.
Actual World Series: C+. Ortiz was absolutely locked in, hitting .688/.760/1.188 with two home runs and eight walks. The Cardinals were so scared of him by Game 6 that they intentionally walked him three times -- with two of those helping lead to rallies and a 6-1 Red Sox victory in the final game.
This one could be No. 25 -- it was during the pandemic, after all, and it was played at a neutral site in a half-empty stadium for social distancing reasons. But it was a great matchup between the teams with the best records in each league, albeit over the shortened 60-game season. You had Mookie Betts and Clayton Kershaw and Randy Arozarena in the midst of one of the best postseasons ever, plus the small-market Rays trying to beat the big-market Dodgers.
Actual World Series: C+. Because teams were allowed an expanded roster of 28 players, it was a parade of relievers -- but there were some fun games, including a bonkers ending to Game 4 and then Rays manager Kevin Cash's controversial decision to remove Blake Snell in Game 6, which backfired in a big way.
Maybe this should rate higher. After all, at the time, the White Sox were trying to break a World Series drought going back to 1917 and the Astros, born in 1962, had never won. But the White Sox's drought never had the same nationwide interest as the ones for the Cubs or Red Sox (fair or not) and these weren't particularly interesting teams. The White Sox were very good -- they won 99 games -- but lacked star power, with Paul Konerko their biggest name (Frank Thomas was on the team that year but played only 34 games and was injured for the playoffs). The Astros had Yankees transplants Roger Clemens and Andy Pettitte, but their two longtime stars, Jeff Bagwell and Craig Biggio, were at the end of their careers (Bagwell, in his final season, was relegated to DH and pinch-hitting duties).
Actual World Series: C. It's hard to give a sweep a decent grade, but all four games were exciting, including Scott Podsednik's walk-off home run in Game 2 (after not hitting a home run all season) and Geoff Blum's go-ahead home run in the 14th inning to win Game 3.
The Phillies were back in the World Series for the first time since 1993 -- and hadn't won since 1980. They featured a powerful offense with Chase Utley, Ryan Howard, Jimmy Rollins and Pat Burrell. The Rays were maybe the unlikeliest World Series team ever: In their 10 previous years of existence, they had not only never had a winning season but had lost at least 90 games in each one. They won 97 games that year behind rookie Evan Longoria and power-hitting first baseman Carlos Peña, with speedsters Carl Crawford and B.J. Upton in the outfield.
Actual World Series: D+. Three games were decided by one run, but it was a pretty uneventful World Series. The lasting memory is the cold and rain in Philly that forced the midgame postponement of Game 5, the only time that has happened in World Series history. The game was suspended in the sixth inning and resumed two days later.
A Subway Series -- the first since the Yankees and Brooklyn Dodgers met in 1956 -- was certainly fun for the Big Apple, but it was less fun for the rest of the country (it drew the worst TV ratings at the time). The Yankees were going for a third straight World Series and had officially become the Evil Empire by that point. To make it even worse, they weren't even that good that season, winning only 87 games. The Mets were back in the World Series for the first time since 1986. There was certainly plenty of star power all around with the likes of Derek Jeter, Roger Clemens and Mike Piazza.
Actual World Series: C+. It was a tight-fought five-game series with all games decided by two runs or fewer. The turning point was the bottom of the ninth of Game 1, when the Yankees tied it off Armando Benitez and went on to win in 12 innings. Game 2 featured the infamous Clemens-Piazza bat-throwing incident, and the Yankees won the clincher with two runs in the ninth off a tired Al Leiter.
I know, the Astros ... again. Boo. But this was an absolute powerhouse of a team with 106 wins and stars such asYordan Alvarez (1.019 OPS) and Verlander (18-4, 1.75 ERA), plus the old standbys Jose Altuve and Alex Bregman. The Phillies, meanwhile, snuck in as a wild-card team for their first playoff trip since 2011 but were an immensely entertaining team with Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber& Co., as well as a passionate fanbase cheering them on.
Actual World Series: C. The Phillies won 6-5 in Game 1 on J.T. Realmuto's home run in the 10th inning. They took a 2-1 series lead, but then their bats died. Astros pitchers tossed a combined no-hitter to even the series, and Houston won the final two games 3-2 and 4-1, with Alvarez's three-run blast in Game 6 the deciding blow.
The Brewers' drought is the big narrative here as they try to finally cash in after their past decade of success, but we're still getting the 103-win Brewers facing the 98-win Rays, the best combined win total in the World Series since the Astros and Dodgers in 2017. (Not to mention we get a first-time winner no matter the outcome.) The Brewers aren't your conventional powerhouse team -- relying on speed, defense, timely hitting and a dominant bullpen -- but they do have one of the biggest stars of the 2026 season in Jacob Misiorowski, plus a rising star in young Jackson Chourio. The Rays might lack big names, although Junior Caminero is just the second player with two 40-homer seasons by age 22, and like the Brewers, they're trying to finally win it all after years of success.
Actual World Series: To be determined.
The Royals proved their 2014 World Series appearance was no fluke, winning 95 games with a better team that included trade deadline additions Ben Zobrist and Johnny Cueto. The Mets won the NL East behind a young, powerful rotation that featured Matt Harvey, Noah Syndergaard and Jacob deGrom. It was a fun matchup of teams trying to avoid lengthy title droughts -- 30 years for the Royals, 29 for the Mets.
Actual World Series: C+. It went only five games, but the Royals won the opener in 14 innings, won Game 5 with a three-run eighth inning and then won the clincher in 12 innings -- after Mets manager Terry Collins' ill-fated decision to leave in Harvey to start the ninth with a 2-0 lead.
This was a super entertaining showdown at the time. The Giants had yet to win a World Series in San Francisco and featured Tim Lincecum ("The Freak," for his small stature and overpowering stuff) and two rookies named Posey and Bumgarner. The Rangers had never won a championship and featured AL MVP Josh Hamilton and veteran DH Vladimir Guerrero. Both teams had pulled off upsets in the LCS, with the Giants beating the Phillies and the Rangers beating the Yankees.
Actual World Series: D. Meh. The Giants won the opener in a blowout as the Rangers made four errors and then tossed shutouts in Games 2 (behind Matt Cain) and 4 (behind Bumgarner). You can test Giants fans by asking them who won World Series MVP honors that year. Answer: Edgar Renteria (he hit .412 with two home runs and six RBIs).
Remember, this happened before the sign-stealing scandal changed how we view this era of the Astros. They had won 107 games behind the pitching duo of Verlander and Gerrit Cole and four players who mashed 30-plus home runs (which didn't even include Alvarez, a rookie that year). The Nationals were a wild-card team that had overcome a 19-31 season start to win 93 games and featured a starting pitching trio of Scherzer, Stephen Strasburg and Patrick Corbin (and 20-year-old sensation Juan Soto, who hit 34 home runs).
Actual World Series: B-. It went seven games -- the road team would win all seven -- although five of the games weren't close. The best game was the last one: The Nationals went ahead 3-2 in the seventh inning on Anthony Rendon's home run and then Howie Kendrick's go-ahead home run just inside the right-field foul pole.
This matchup began with a lot of hype: Shohei Ohtani, coming off his all-time game in the NLCS in which he hit three home runs and struck out 10 batters as the starting pitcher, against Vladimir Guerrero Jr., who had hit .442 with six home runs through the first two rounds of the playoffs. The Dodgers were looking to become the first team with back-to-back titles since the 2000 Yankees and the first NL team since the 1976 Reds. The Blue Jays were back in the World Series for the first time since Joe Carter walked off the Phillies in 1993. Dodgers manager Dave Roberts stirred things up after the NLCS when he said during the postgame celebration, "Let's get four more wins and really ruin baseball" -- a reference to the criticism of the Dodgers' high payroll.
Actual World Series: A+. The Dodgers won Game 3 in 18 innings on Freddie Freeman's walk-off home run, which followed an unlikely four-inning relief performance from Will Klein, the last guy on the Dodgers' staff. The Dodgers went back to Toronto trailing 3-2 but won Game 6 behind Yoshinobu Yamamoto and a crazy game-ending double play.
Game 7 featured two future Hall of Famers starting in Ohtani and Max Scherzer, more on-the-edge-of-your-seat plays than any game in World Series history, Miguel Rojas' unlikely home run in the ninth to tie it, as well as Will Smith's go-ahead one in the 11th -- and finally, Yamamoto pitching in relief to close out the game by inducing a double play with two runners on to win it for the Dodgers. It wasn't quite the greatest World Series overall, but two all-time games made it a classic.
The Angels, who joined the majors in 1961, were making their first World Series appearance, while the Giants, in the Bay Area since 1958, were trying to win their first title since moving from New York. You had Barry Bonds at the height of his unstoppable powers -- and trying to erase his own postseason demons -- while the Angels had a loaded lineup (Troy Glaus, Tim Salmon, Garret Anderson), the Rally Monkey and those deafening ThunderStix (let us pray they never return).
Actual World Series: A. Bonds was a beast, hitting .471/.700/1.294 (yes, that's a 1.994 OPS), but it wasn't enough. This series featured four one-run games, including a wild 11-10 contest and the classic Game 6, when the Angels rallied late from a 5-0 deficit to win 6-5. Game 7 was a drab 4-1 contest (Bonds went a harmless 1-for-3).
The Yankees had missed the playoffs in 2008 for the first time since 1993, so they went out and signed free agents CC Sabathia, Mark Teixeira and A.J. Burnett to add to an already stacked roster that included Jeter, Alex Rodriguez, Robinson Cano, Hideki Matsui, Jorge Posada and Johnny Damon. Whoa. Yes, they were still the Evil Empire. The Phillies, trying to defend their title, had traded for Cliff Lee and then signed Pedro Martinez in July to bolster their rotation.
Actual World Series: C. It could have been a classic battle, but there were no one-run games and Game 6 -- Martinez's final start of his career -- was over early. The crucial contest was Game 4, when the Yankees scored three runs in the ninth off Phillies closer Brad Lidge to win 7-4.
This one presented conflicting emotions. The Yankees were going for an unthinkable fourth straight title, but in the wake of 9/11, there was a "Win it for New York" angle that the Yankees had never encountered. The Diamondbacks, meanwhile, had the big, bad duo of Randy Johnson and Curt Schilling, with Schilling, when asked on the eve of the World Series about the Yankees' mystique and aura, giving one of the great quips in World Series history: "Mystique and Aura? Those are dancers at a nightclub." The Diamondbacks were not going to be intimidated.
Actual World Series: A+. Four one-run games, including three of the most memorable World Series moments ever: Jeter's Mr. November home run to win Game 4, Scott Brosius' walk-off home run to win Game 5 and then Luis Gonzalez's bloop single to beat the invincible Mariano Rivera in Game 7.
Two of baseball's most historic franchises had never met in a World Series, creating the classic showdown with games in Fenway Park and Dodger Stadium. It doesn't get any better than that. The Red Sox were a 108-win powerhouse -- with AL MVP Mookie Betts leading the way, backed up by J.D. Martinez, who hit .330 with 43 home runs that season. Chris Sale and David Price headlined the rotation. The Dodgers actually had a bit of a down year with 92 wins, but they also weren't lacking in big names, with Manny Machado (a trade deadline acquisition), Yasiel Puig, Matt Kemp, Cody Bellinger and Justin Turner, with Kershaw and rookie Walker Buehler on the pitching side.
Actual World Series: C-. A letdown. The first two games in Fenway were cold and windy. Game 3 was an 18-inning affair -- longest in World Series history -- but was more of a slog than a game to remember. Game 4 was the best of the series as the Red Sox rallied with nine runs over the final three innings to win 9-6.
This series had it all: dominant teams (both won over 100 games), long World Series title droughts (never for the Astros, 1988 for the Dodgers) and superstars galore (Altuve, Verlander, Carlos Correa, Kershaw, Seager, Bellinger, Yu Darvish). We didn't know at the time that both franchises were just kicking off 100-win dynasties -- let alone what the Astros were doing behind the scenes -- but the anticipation level was off the charts for the first matchup of 100-win teams in the World Series since 1970.
Actual World Series: A-. Game 1, with a start-time temperature of 103 degrees at Dodger Stadium, was a Kershaw 11-strikeout gem. The Astros tied Game 2 in the ninth on Marwin Gonzalez's home run off Kenley Jansen (1.32 ERA that season), both teams scored twice in the 10th, the Astros scored twice in the 11th on George Springer's home run and held on for a 7-6 win. Game 4 featured a five-run rally in the ninth by the Dodgers to win. Game 5 was completely bananas, with the Astros finally winning 13-12 in 10 innings. Game 7 was a letdown though, as the Astros won a 5-1 snoozer in which they scored five runs off Darvish in the first two innings.
As mentioned, what's not to like? Aside from Ohtani and Judge each playing in their first World Series and trying to put a final stamp on their legacy-defining seasons, we have Juan Soto and Mookie Betts, a suddenly rejuvenated Giancarlo Stanton and a hobbled Freddie Freeman (only raising the drama if he hits well), Gerrit Cole and Yoshinobu Yamamoto. Aside from the history between the clubs, we have both clubs needing to rewrite their recent history: The Yankees, back in the World Series for the first time since 2009, and the Dodgers trying to add a more legitimate championship to the one they won in the COVID-shortened season.
Actual World Series:C+. The Judge-Ohtani showdown was a flop, as Judge hit .222 with one home run and Ohtani hit .105 without a home run or RBI. The series also went just five games, with the Dodgers winning the first three. The series did produce two forever moments, however: Freddie Freeman's walk-off, Kirk Gibson-esque grand slam in Game 1 and the Yankees' fifth-inning defensive meltdown in Game 5.
The Red Sox were coming off their never-done-before comeback from down 3-0 to beat the Yankees in the ALCS -- and still had to beat a 105-win Cardinals team that featured Pujols (.331, 46 home runs), Jim Edmonds (.301, 42 home runs) and Scott Rolen (.314, 34 home runs), plus in-season pickup Larry Walker, who had an OPS over 1.000 that year. The Red Sox had their own ridiculous lineup with Ortiz (.301, 41 home runs), Ramirez (.308, 43 home runs) and Damon (.304, 20 home runs) plus a rotation with Schilling and Martinez. It seems inevitable now that Boston was going to win, but that wasn't the case at the time, so the buildup was intense.
Actual World Series: D. Blah. I mean, Red Sox fans will rightfully call it the best World Series ever, but after a sloppy 11-9 Game 1 played in a drizzle at Fenway (the Red Sox won despite committing four errors), the Cardinals never led again.
The Cubs had not only not won since 1908, but they hadn't even been in a World Series since 1945. The Guardians, meanwhile, had the second-longest drought of the original 16 teams, without a title since 1948. That was enough right there to build up the anticipation, but this also rates high because it was two good teams -- Chicago won 104 games while Cleveland won 94. Cubs third baseman Kris Bryant won MVP honors that year and Cleveland was led by 18-game winner Corey Kluber (who would start three times) and young rising stars Francisco Lindor and Jose Ramirez.
Actual World Series: B. The first six games weren't anything too special, but Game 7 was one of the greatest in World Series history. Cleveland tied it on Rajai Davis' three-run homer in the bottom of the eighth, the Cubs scored twice in the 10th -- following a stress-filled rain delay -- and escaped with an 8-7, curse-ending win when Cleveland had to bat little-used Michael Martinez with its season on the line.

item.content:encoded:
In some universe out there, Nick Offerman has a son, and he's a nasty left-handed pitcher for the Boston Red Sox. At least, that's how Offerman sees it.
The Chicago Cubs fan, actor and comedian who plays Ron Swanson (Parks and Rec) appeared on "The Joy of Baseball" podcast. He praised Payton Tolle for the skills and fun he brings to the game, and also took full credit for the mustache, joking that he could be his father. Tolle fired back with "Come to my arms papa," on social media which might be the most exciting Red Sox news of the offseason, so far.
If you hadn't noticed the resemblance before now, I'm sorry for pointing it out, because you won't be able to unsee it. When you put the two side by side you really need a DNA test to tell them and the mustaches apart.
I visited High-A Greenville last year, and Drive general manager Eric Jarinko told me he was the most impressive pitcher he'd ever seen, and one of the coolest, most down-to-earth guys, too.
Tolle is doing his part to fit in with the Red Sox, not just on the field but in Red Sox facial hair history, as well. Facial hair has always been part of the Red Sox identity, so we found the most iconic mustaches ever worn in a Sox uniform. We mostly stuck to household names and ranked them on accolades, history and a few personal connections. If you want to go down the rabbit hole yourself, this isn't the first time BoSox Injection has shown love to Red Sox mustaches — we covered the subject back in 2014, and for Sox fans this list gets really in the weeds, enjoy.
10 of the most iconic mustaches in Red Sox history as Payton Tolle keeps the tradition going
Luis Tiant
El Tiante gets the top spot because he wore No. 23, the number I was going to wear before I was traded from the Red Sox (I even had to ask for his blessing) and he was still rocking the stache then. The handlebar went with a one-of-a-kind windup, and he won 20 or more games three times in Boston.
Payton Tolle
The personality, the parted pencil mustache Over the Monster called "a statement," and the electric stuff are why he ranks this high. He went 9-6 with a 3.03 ERA and 171 strikeouts this year, and is officially endorsed by Offerman.
Dwight Evans
"Dewey" played in Boston from 1972 to 1990 and grew the mustache in the '80s as he became one of the AL's top hitters. He later served as a special advisor to the general manager and was always around spring training when I was there, a super nice, soft-spoken guy.
Wade Boggs
I grew up a Yankee fan, so I remember him clean-shaven in pinstripes. But I always heard how historic he was in Boston, along with the reputation: allegedly 64 beers on a flight, and fried chicken before every game.
Jerry Remy
RemDawg's mustache followed him from second base to the NESN booth, and he was part of the NESN crew. He's got to get some love.
Dennis Eckersley
He went 20-8 with a 2.99 ERA in his first Boston season, then reinvented himself as an electric closer on his way to Cooperstown. He also broadcast for NESN and is deeply missed in the booth.
Jim Rice
Rice hit 382 homers, won the 1978 AL MVP, and kept the mustache through all of it.
Alex Bregman
His Tom Selleck-style mustache lasted until June 6, 2025, when he shaved it between innings against the Yankees to spark a rally. It didn't work, but it's an iconic moment in modern Red Sox pop culture.
Garrett Richards
He started his in 2020 when the pandemic shut down camp, and he told WEEI, "My wife absolutely hates it, bless her heart." A Boston radio show challenged him to curl the ends up Rollie Fingers-style.
Bill Buckner
This is not a slight, because most Red Sox fans have a sour taste in their mouths, but he shouldn't be reduced to one grounder. He had 2,715 hits and a 1980 batting title, and the mustache deserves better than a footnote.
Honorable mentions go to Rod Beck's fu manchu, Tony Armas' afro-and-mustache combo and Jody Reed, whose lip helped start that 2014 list in the first place.
The 2013 beard era took over Boston's upper lip for a while, but mustaches are creeping back, and Tolle has one of the best in baseball right now. This franchise has never been short on characters, from Tiant's windup to Bregman's mid-game shave. Pedro Martinez called Tolle "a bully," and he fits right in. If he keeps this up, he could be a face of this franchise for years, and the mustache will be right there with him.

item.content:encoded:
When Boston Red Sox fans reminisce on the greatest Red Sox players in franchise history, Pedro Martinez and David Ortiz both come to mind quite quickly. They were instrumental in breaking the Curse and bringing the 2004 World Series title to Boston after nearly a century-long drought.
Martinez and Ortiz are both Hall of Famers and fan-favorites — the Red Sox haven't had two stars of their caliber at the same time since their retirement. Little did most Sox fans know, they never would've had one without the other.
In an interview with Bleacher Report and TNT Sports, Martinez explained his part in bringing Ortiz to Boston before the 2003 season — and it's significant. The two players saw each other at a restaurant in the offseason, the day Ortiz was released by the Minnesota Twins. Martinez then committed to making Ortiz a Red Sox.
"I ended up calling [Larry] Lucchino, Theo [Epstein] and everybody and everybody. And I couldn't get ahold of them. They were in the Winter Meeting trying to sign a first baseman," Martinez said. "I'm pushing the phone to see if I can get David in before they make a decision. I finally get ahold of the traveling secretary, Jack McCormick... I said... 'I just want the Red Sox to pick up David. He just got released and I don't want any other team to see him.'"
Pedro Martinez reveals that he recruited David Ortiz to Red Sox, beginning a legendary partnership
And, lucky for Boston, no other team did. After Ortiz's release from the Twins, Martinez helped him become one of the most iconic and clutch Red Sox players of all time.
Ortiz played six years in Minnesota before his move to Boston and he was hardly a household name. He slashed .266/.348/.461 with 108 doubles and 58 home runs over parts of six seasons. All 10 of Ortiz's All-Star nods and his seven Silver Slugger awards came after his move to Boston shocked his career to life.
Martinez in the interview said he saw Ortiz's potential after Ortiz took one of his cutters to the upper deck of the Metrodome. The Red Sox organization and Fenway Park helped Ortiz flex that potential like he never had before — he batted .290/.386/.570 with 524 doubles, 483 home runs and 1,530 RBI over his illustrious 14-year career in Boston. He earned MVP votes in eight of his 14 years with the Sox. He was impossibly clutch, carrying Boston to two more World Series wins without Martinez.
But maybe there is no "without Martinez." If over two decades ago two of the most legendary Red Sox in franchise history didn't happen to be in "the right place at the right time," as Martinez said, the Curse might still be active. Ortiz could've been an icon of a different franchise, if he became one at all. Martinez has quite an eye for excellence.

Thursday night Pedro Martinez stopped by Fenway Park, and while making the rounds the Red Sox legend held court in the back of the press box to talk about the team, his day working with elementary school students in Lawrence earlier in the afternoon, and the upcoming Red Sox-Yankees playoff rematch.
But before wrapping up, he addressed one other matter close to his heart.
Toronto Blue Jays slugger Vladimir Guerrero Jr., whose Hall of Fame father played with Martinez with the Montreal Expos and was a fellow Dominican Republic great, recently raised eyebrows when he made comments in a Spanish-language interview suggesting that his 14-year, $500 million contract was a reward for past performance and not an investment by the Blue Jays into his future potential.
“I want people to understand one thing,” Guerrero said in Spanish, per MLB.com’s translation. “The money they gave me wasn’t for what I’m going to do. It was for what I already did. They didn’t pay me because I’m going to hit 40 every year. They paid me for what I already accomplished. People are confused about that, but I think the same way they do. Like, sometimes I even say to myself: bro, they gave you all that money and you’re out here doing nothing. I try.”
Those remarks drew criticism from Blue Jays fans and from across the sport, but Martinez, who is Guerrero’s godfather, said he believes his comments were widely misinterpreted.
“What he meant was he’s got a contract probably because of the things he did and what he might do in the future,” Martinez said. “That’s a young man talking that didn’t really explain himself, he got paid based on what he did and what he might do in the future, it’s a projection.”
While Guerrero initially stood by his comments when asked on Wednesday, he addressed the matter again on Friday and apologized to fans for the impression he’d given. He said he’d also spoken to Blue Jays manager John Schneider and apologized to his teammates for the distraction the whole ordeal had caused.
“I just gave it some thought, and I felt like the comments I made the other day were not really what I wanted to say,” Guerrero said, per Keegan Matheson of MLB.com. “I felt that everyone, my fans and everyone, deserves an apology from me.”
The firestorm comes amid a disappointing season for Guerrero, who is already a six-time All-Star at age 27 and helped lead the Blue Jays to within inches of a World Series championship last fall. But after averaging nearly 32 home runs per year over his last five seasons, Guerrero has hit only nine homers this year to go along with a massive drop in production across the board.
The Blue Jays, initially a favorite to repeat as American League champions, missed the playoffs and will finish with a losing record.
Schneider stood up for Guerrero as a teammate and a leader, and Martinez, who has known Guerrero since he was a young boy, vouched for his character, insisting that he isn’t the type of person who’d rest on his laurels.
“Vlad is not that arrogant guy that’s going to be saying ‘ahh I got paid and that’s it and I’m going to sit down,’ no, Vlady’s a gamer! We all know it,” Martinez said. “So don’t let those people that want to really ruin a good player get to that point.”
Pedro on Tracy, Breslow
Among his comments Thursday, Martinez also offered high praise for Red Sox manager Chad Tracy and chief baseball officer Craig Breslow, who both recently received long-term job security that will keep them leading the organization through the end of the decade.
Tracy, the Hall of Famer said, has done a great job pressing all the right buttons and getting the most out of his young players.
“Outstanding. Outstanding. You couldn’t ask for more. If you asked for more you’re being greedy,” Martinez said. “This is a guy that quietly, under the table, has done what he needs to do, not that Alex (Cora) didn’t do it because we saw Alex do an outstanding job, but the young team that we have has somehow clicked with him.”
Martinez also was a fan of the moves Breslow made at the trade deadline to help bolster the club’s roster ahead of the playoff push.
“Breslow deserves a lot of credit for the movement he made during the deadline, for how everything is working, for the entire team and the organization,” Martinez said. “We have to give to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and so far the job has been done right.”
Big fan of Tolle
Since debuting for the Red Sox late in the 2025 season, Payton Tolle has endeared himself to Red Sox fans through both his dominant performances on the mound and his larger-than-life personality.
He’s won over Martinez too, who said he loves how Tolle pitches with such infectious energy and wishes he could have learned to embrace that kind of attitude during his playing days.
“I wish I could teach myself at an early age how to be like Tolle,” Martinez said. “The guy laughs, the guy pitches, the guy is a bully, the guy is big and intimidating, he’s got everything.”
Martinez said he appreciates guys like Tolle and New York Mets reliever Jefry Yan — who often performs a dramatic jumping celebration after each strikeout — for what they bring to the game. Martinez was famously as no nonsense as you could possibly be during his playing career, but despite their apparent differences Martinez also appreciates the edge Tolle pitches with as well.
“At the same time he’s out there to beat you,” Martinez said. “He’s a bully. I love him, I love him, and he’s aware of everything he’s doing, even though he’s laughing and goofing around, you see him graciously, I think he’s doing what he needs to do and even more, having fun with it, something I couldn’t do.”

Por Alexander Gómez
La Fundación Pedro Martínez amplió su trabajo educativo en Massachusetts y República Dominicana con un programa de programación, videojuegos e inteligencia artificial que beneficiará a estudiantes de siete escuelas de Lawrence, Massachusetts.
“Nosotros creemos que el conocimiento es lo que da autoridad y cuando al ser humano podemos facilitarle herramientas para enfrentar la vida, pues es más fácil”, afirmó Carolina, quien explicó que el proyecto comenzó hace tres años y contempla alumnos de tercer y cuarto grado.
Por su parte, Pedro Martínez exhortó a la juventud latina a trabajar por sus propios objetivos y a convertirse en agentes de progreso dentro de sus comunidades, al destacar el valor de servir de ejemplo para las nuevas generaciones.
“La voz que escuchan es un vivo ejemplo de lo que nosotros podemos ser. No le estoy pidiendo que sean precisamente como yo o como Carolina, sino como ellos quieran ser”, afirmó Martínez durante al ser entrevistados por Nilson Pepén en la transmisión en español de los Medias Rojas de Boston.
Martínez, miembro del Salón de la Fama y una de las figuras dominicanas más identificadas con Boston, dijo sentirse honrado de poder representar un modelo para los jóvenes latinos y contribuir al crecimiento de la comunidad hispana.
“Que sean alguien y que ayuden a seguir trayendo nuestra comunidad latina al sendero más alto que podamos encontrar”, expresó. El exlanzador también resaltó el avance de la presencia latina en Boston desde su llegada a la ciudad en 1998 y su satisfacción por haber formado parte de ese proceso.

When Pedro Martinez was on the mound for the Boston Red Sox, he was a fan favorite.
More than 20 years later, as schoolchildren cheered and swarmed around him for autographs Thursday in Lawrence, Massachusetts, it was clear that has not changed.
The baseball Hall of Famer's childhood struggles continue to inspire his commitment to giving back. Martinez and his wife, Carolina, are launching a new afterschool coding program serving seven elementary schools in Lawrence.
"I had to struggle for everything I achieved in life, and I just want to make it easier for others to get to where I got," Martinez said.
The program will give hundreds of third- and fourth-grade students access to modern technology and opportunities to develop coding and problem-solving skills.
"Maybe because it's something I was denied when I was younger," Martinez said when asked why the program is so important to him.
Martinez spoke with students at Lawrence schools as part of a back-to-school celebration, where children also received school supplies and gift bags.
The program is focused on reaching students early, Carolina Martinez said.
"Their age mattered to us in terms of the decision, because the earlier you get them, the more motivated they're going to be, but also, the more resourceful they're going to be later on," she said.
South Lawrence East Elementary School Principal Lori Butterfield said students are already immersed in technology, and the program will help them move from simply using technology to creating with it.
"They love playing games. They love using apps. They're using AI all the time. I want them to learn how to create those things, and I think this program will allow them to do that," Butterfield said.
For Martinez, the connection to Lawrence is personal.
"Why? Because in Lawrence, I quickly identified the need, I found my culture, I found my people here. I found my roots," he said.
Martinez also reflected on what can happen when young people are given even one opportunity.
"Remember, what you're seeing right now is the product of an opportunity. Only one, and that's all it took," he said.
Martinez seized his own opportunities on the mound, becoming one of baseball's most accomplished pitchers.
With the Red Sox preparing to face the Yankees in the postseason, Martinez was asked how he would feel about taking the mound today.
"I'll be ready from here, to give them all the knowledge and everything, all the experience I've done before — I'm ready to do that any day," he said. "But physically, to go pitch? I have Payton Tolle and I have Sonny Gray to go do it for me."
Martinez said he plans to continue coming back to Lawrence and contributing to the community — a place he now considers home.

Many of us believe he’s the best pitcher we’ve ever seen. He’s a blue-chip, first-ballot Hall of Famer, part of the Red Sox team that broke the Curse, and seen on TBS after Sox playoff games in any given October. He’ll be 55 next month and spends every year shuttling between Boston and his native Dominican Republic, when he’s not working in Atlanta. He has no regrets about saying “The Yankees are my daddy,” all those years ago, and he thinks the Red Sox have a shot to beat the Yankees in New York next week.
He is the one and only Pedro Martinez, and he’s spending Thursday in Lawrence with his wife, Carolina, launching an after-school coding program at South Lawrence East Elementary School, then engaging in a question-and-answer session with hundreds of students at Lawrence High School.
“Lawrence has been kind of forgotten a little bit,” said Martinez. “It has gotten kind of old in front of our eyes, but there is so much need. If there’s something I can really identify myself with, it is need. I grew up in those kind of needs. I’m just expressing the cry I had when I was a kid. I get excited every time I see a kid that has an opportunity to become someone.”
Martinez’s new program is designed to bridge resource gaps and enhance classroom learning for young students across Lawrence. His foundation, dedicated to transforming the lives of youth in the United States and the Dominican Republic, was started in 1998 when he joined the Sox after five-plus stellar seasons with the Dodgers and Expos.
“I got a very pleasant surprise when I got to Fenway as soon as I saw the drums and the people with the [Dominican] flag and the atmosphere kind of changing,” Martinez recalled. “Mayor [Thomas] Menino was kind enough to take me in his SUV to give me a tour around Boston, and right away I fell in love with the people … and the Latino community all over the place, and that’s when I landed in Lawrence, Lynn, Dorchester, and all those areas that continue to be linked to me.”
It was in those early Boston days that Martinez’s Fenway mound starts “became the curfew back home in the Dominican every time I pitched.”
A connection was made; an ongoing, lasting relationship because of the Pedro Martinez Foundation.
In 2026, Martinez and teammate/countryman David Ortiz are listed as “special assistants” in the fourth line of the the Red Sox’ official front office directory, just below chief baseball officer Craig Breslow. Martinez occasionally helps young Sox pitchers at spring training, but he was out of the loop when the decision was made to fire manager Alex Cora and six coaches just 27 games into the season.
“I was actually talking to Alex a couple of days before,” Martinez remembered. “When I found out, I wasn’t angry, I just couldn’t understand how everything snowballed to that point.”
Martinez’s beloved former teammate, catcher/captain Jason Varitek, was part of the purge. The Sox claimed Varitek was “reassigned,” but he hasn’t surfaced anywhere in the organization.
Does Martinez think the burned bridge will be repaired?
“I think it’s going to be OK with Jason,” said the three-time Cy Young Award winner. “Jason is a very professional person. He understands that business part, just like Alex Cora.”
What does Martinez think about the local demonization of Rafael Devers?
“This is a very misunderstood kid,” he said. “Devers is very shy. But he is legit. He’s a guy that doesn’t know how to express himself and has a hard time trusting anybody but his father. His father knows the actual truth … Devers is very respectful, a very lovely kid, but now it’s over and the team is on its way to success. … You have to learn to love Boston if you want to survive in Boston. Boston is 24/7 talking about their sports.”
Does Martinez want Payton Tolle or Sonny Gray starting Game 1?
“You don’t go wrong with either one,” he said. “Sonny is a true professional, a true competitor. I love, love Tolle. Just his amazing attitude. I love every single pitch he throws. I love everything about him.
“The Yankees are vulnerable, especially without [Aaron] Judge. I don’t think the Red Sox are intimidated by the Yankees. I think they can beat not only the Yankees but any team in baseball.”
The highlight of Martinez’s baseball career?
“Being part of the 25 that brought the trophy to Boston.”
Ever wish he never said, “The Yankees are my daddy”?
“No. I was being honest. That’s what you guys demand from all of us. The Yankees had my number at that point, and I expressed it. I will tell you in the most honest way, I got my ass kicked.”
Which brings us back to 2003, when Grady Little was fired (almost immediately) after failing to take Martinez out of the game when Pedro was past his pitch limit after seven innings of Game 7 of the ALCS at Yankee Stadium. Martinez had fanned Alfonso Soriano on his final pitch of the seventh, was at 100 pitches, and believed he was done for the night.
“[Red Sox pitching coach] Dave Wallace told me I was done after, so I didn’t put my jacket on,” said Martinez. “I had looked up in the sky and gave thanks to God for the seven innings I pitched. Our bullpen was lights out. All of a sudden Grady was like, ‘I don’t like [Alan] Embree against Nick Johnson in the eighth.’ He said, ‘You give me Nick Johnson and I got the rest of the bullpen for you.’ That’s the true story.”
Back on the mound, leading, 5-2, in the eighth, Martinez retired Johnson on a second-pitch popup to start the inning, then looked to the dugout. Nobody moved.
“Nothing happened,” recalled Martinez. “So I just kept going. I gave up a couple of line drives, and everything just snowballed after that. I thought I made a great pitch on [Jorge] Posada, but Posada blooped it [for a two-run double].”
All in all, it was four straight hits and a tie game before Little finally pulled Martinez after 23 disastrous eighth-inning pitches. Then Aaron Boone (now the Yankees’ manager) happened in the 11th.
Two summers ago, Maryland congressman Jamie Raskin wrote President Joe Biden a letter, imploring America’s tiring leader to end his reelection campaign. As part of his logic, Raskin compared Biden’s career to Martinez’s Game 7 performance, writing that there is “no shame in taking a well-deserved bow … when your arm is tired out.”
Days later, Biden pulled out of the race.
“I don’t know what to tell you about that,” chuckled Martinez. “Grady just told me, ‘Get one more out.’ That was Nick Johnson, right?”
Right.
All these years later, the wounds have healed and Martinez is on a greater mission, taking his message to Lawrence.
“I don’t have enough words to describe how grateful I am to have my opportunity through baseball and make a difference now,” said Martinez. “My message to these kids in Lawrence is that nothing in life is too far away if you have the will, if you have the passion.”
Dan Shaughnessy is a Globe columnist. He can be reached at daniel.shaughnessy@globe.com. Follow him @dan_shaughnessy.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are in the middle of a series with the Tampa Bay Rays, but they’ve already clinched a postseason spot, which is set to begin next week.
It seems they just about know exactly what seed they’ll have and who they’ll play as well.
One Tampa Bay win over New York would clinch the AL East for the Rays, which would then slot the Yankees as the top Wild Card team and, as of right now, have them hosting a best-of-three series against the Boston Red Sox next week.
Yankees Will Likely Be Without Judge
Prior to Tuesday’s doubleheader, Yankees manager Aaron Boone revealed that he does not expect Judge to return for the Wild Card series next week due to his calf injury.
He received an injection in his calf this week, and the diagnosis was a moderate calf strain.
“We’re planning on him not being a part of that,” Boone said.
Aaron Judge is likely out for the AL Wild Card Series vs. Boston. “We’re planning on him not being a part of that,” Aaron Boone said.
Judge had a PPP injection in his right calf during the off-day.
— Bryan Hoch ⚾️ (@BryanHoch) September 22, 2026
This now makes it all the more important for the Yankees’ depleted offense to have their starting rotation hold down the fort, which it has done all season long, headlined by Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole, Carlos Rodon, Max Fried, and Will Warren.
Pedro Martinez Makes Suggestion for Yankees
One of the biggest questions facing the Yankees is how they plan to structure a shortened rotation come playoff time, and Hall of Fame pitcher and MLB on TBS analyst Pedro Martinez believes he knows exactly how they should use their core pitchers.
“For the Yankees’ pitching rotation, I’d go with Schlittler first, Rodon second, and Cole third,” Martinez posted on X.
For the Yankees’ pitching rotation, I’d go with Schlittler first, Rodón second, and Cole third. #mlbontbs
— Pedro Martinez (@45PedroMartinez) September 22, 2026
You’re not going to pitch all five starters. That’s just not realistic. With the potential for more off days, you’re going to want your best arms available.
While Schlittler is an obvious no-brainer. Boone will have to decide whether he wants to go with a three-man group or extend it to four and have both Rodon and Fried start, rather than moving one of them to the bullpen alongside Warren, which seems like the most likely outcome for now.

item.content:encoded:
As we make our way through the final week of the regular season, there doesn't seem to be much suspense as to who will be named MVP. At least, that's what we can glean from our latest -- and final -- MLB.com 2026 MVP poll.
Yordan Alvarez is still well out in front in the American League despite relatively mediocre production of late. In the National League, Pete Crow-Armstrong is wrapping up one of the best all-around seasons in recent memory.
Thirty-eight MLB.com experts cast votes for who they think will earn MVP honors after this season, with 32 players receiving at least one vote. As a reminder, votes were based not only on results so far, but also on how things are expected to play out the rest of the season.
Voters ranked their top five picks in each league on a 5-4-3-2-1 scale -- five points for a first-place vote, four points for a second-place vote and so on. Here are the results.
All stats are through Sunday unless otherwise noted.
AMERICAN LEAGUE
Alvarez has been so good this year that what qualifies as a slump for him would be a good stretch for most other hitters. Over his past 41 games, he is hitting .264 with an .840 OPS. Again, not bad for most, but well below the standard of the AL leader in average (.313) and OPS (1.027). Alvarez has three homers and five RBIs through 16 games this month, leaving him tied with the O's Pete Alonso and one home run behind the Rays' Junior Caminero for the AL lead and nine RBIs behind Alonso for the top spot in that statistic. Even though his Triple Crown chances have faded, Alvarez has still put together an awesome 2026 at the plate. His 179 wRC+ is at least 27 points better than any other qualified hitter.
We know Caminero is one of the game's great sluggers. He is finishing up his second straight 40-homer season and swings harder than anyone. But what's been most impressive about his season is his improved strike-zone judgment. He has upped his walk rate from a below-average 6.3% to 11.5%, which ranks in the 80th percentile of MLB. He's also maintained a very solid strikeout rate (18.5%). He's not chasing as much, has shaved his whiff rate and is making more contact overall. That blend of patience, power and bat control is a special combination, especially in a 23-year-old player. Carrying a .363 on-base percentage (52 points better than last season), Caminero's .892 OPS ranks third in the AL.
Witt has had better offensive seasons, although 18 homers, 43 steals and a 119 wRC+ in 137 games is not too shabby. But when you consider his entire skill set, Witt remains extremely valuable. His +16 fielding run value is tied for third in the Majors, and his 22 outs above average tops the AL. He also has a +8 baserunning run value, one behind the D-backs' Corbin Carroll for the MLB lead. So while he hasn't been as undeniable in the batter's box as he was in 2024 (169 wRC+), Witt's all-around greatness has him atop the AL FanGraphs WAR leaderboard (6.6) and in line for a possible top-five finish in the MVP voting for the third time in three years.
There has been quite a bit of MVP chatter surrounding Schlittler in recent weeks. And why not? He is pacing the AL in ERA (1.94), WHIP (0.91) and FanGraphs pitching WAR (6.1). He ranks second in the junior circuit in opponents' batting average (.182) and strikeout-minus-walk rate (25.0%). He has allowed one or zero runs in 21 starts. That's a Yankees franchise record and something only two other pitchers age-25 or younger have accomplished in the Live Ball Era (since 1920): Blake Snell (2018) and Dean Chance (1964). He seems like a lock for the AL Cy Young Award at this point, but Schlittler will receive his fair share of MVP love.
Schlittler hasn't been the only indispensable Yankee this year. While New York has been without Aaron Judge for a large portion of the season and has missed other star bats as well due to injuries, Rice has been a constant. He ranks third in the AL in homers (39) and runs scored (100). He's fourth in the league in RBIs (95) and OPS (.888), and tied for fourth in batting run value (+34). With two homers during the final week, Rice would become just the second non-Judge Yankee over the past decade to hit at least 41 homers in a season, joining Juan Soto (2024).
Others receiving votes: Willson Contreras, Red Sox; Pete Alonso, Orioles; Kevin McGonigle, Tigers; Miguel Vargas, White Sox; Randy Arozarena, Mariners; Munetaka Murakami, White Sox; Dylan Cease, Blue Jays
NATIONAL LEAGUE
Last month, PCA jumped over Ohtani and into the No. 1 spot in our poll. This month, he has run away from the rest of the field. The recipient of every first-place vote cast by our panel, Crow-Armstrong is tied with Kyle Schwarber for the MLB lead in home runs (45). No one has more runs (118), extra-base hits (83) or total bases (351) this season. With 38 steals, the Cubs' dynamic center fielder could become the seventh member of the 40-40 club later this week. Oh, and let's not overlook the fact that he is arguably the best defensive player at any position right now. It's no longer a question of whether Crow-Armstrong is the NL MVP. The award is as good as his right now. But will he win it in unanimous fashion?
Ohtani remains the clear runner-up in the NL despite playing in just three games this month due to his nagging left knee and right biceps injuries. The good news is Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said "there's a good chance" Ohtani will be activated from the 15-day injured list Wednesday after a minimum stint. He won't pitch for the rest of the season, leaving him with a 1.79 ERA and 95 K's over 85 2/3 innings. But Ohtani will have a few games to add to his offensive totals (30 homers, 142 wRC+).
We mentioned earlier how Schlittler looks like the heavy favorite for the AL Cy Young Award. Misiorowski is an even bigger shoo-in in the senior circuit. Through 169 1/3 innings, Miz leads the Majors in just about every category, including ERA (1.86), WHIP (0.80), strikeout-minus-walk rate (31.7%) and fWAR (6.5), to name just a few. Opposing batters have a scant .474 OPS against Misiorowski, which is the second-lowest by any qualified starter in the Divisional Era (since 1969). Pedro Martinez, in one of the greatest seasons by a pitcher, recorded a .473 opponents' OPS in 2000.
De La Cruz, who didn't receive a single vote in our previous MVP poll, has been red-hot for Cincinnati over the past month. In his last 27 games, he is batting .404 with eight homers, six steals and a 1.205 OPS. He collected multiple hits in 14 of those games, and his 2.5 fWAR during this period is the best in the big leagues. This prolonged hot streak has given De La Cruz a career-best 139 wRC+ and has left him two homers and two steals away from becoming the fourth Red in the 30-30 club and the first since Brandon Phillips in 2007.
Schwarber has fallen into a bit of a rut, going 4-for-34 with one home run over his past 10 games. He's also eight strikeouts away from setting a new record for K's in a single season. Even so, you have to admire Schwarber's consistency. He will end up with more than 40 homers and 150 games played in four of the past five seasons. He has surpassed 100 walks for a fourth consecutive season, and a third NL home run title is right there for the taking, too.
Others receiving votes: Fernando Tatis Jr., Padres; Brice Turang, Brewers; Matt Olson, Braves; James Wood, Nationals; Jordan Walker, Cardinals; Alex Bregman, Cubs; Bryce Harper, Phillies; Jake Bauers, Brewers; Otto Lopez, Marlins; Gabriel Moreno, Diamondbacks; Rafael Devers, Giants; Alec Burleson, Cardinals; CJ Abrams, Nationals; Corbin Carroll, Diamondbacks; Cristopher Sánchez, Phillies

item.content:encoded:
If you're not already a card collector, Red Sox fans, here's the quick version of what product sports cards enthusiasts are going crazy over right now. Bowman Chrome is Topps' flagship prospect release, the one product every year built specifically around getting a player's first-ever card into the hobby before he's played a single big-league game. Think of it like a company's IPO. It's the first moment the public gets to invest or collect a piece of a player’s career, before anyone really knows what it'll become.
That's the appeal, and it's also the risk. Some of these names turn into stars. Some never sniff the majors at all. Either way, this is the top of the sports card market right now, and some of these prices have gotten astronomical. You have to truly believe in these prospects to justify what you're paying for a shot at them.
The 1st Bowman class, Roman Anthony rookie cards, and how to collect Red Sox legends
Boston has four 1st Bowman cards this year, all likely the cheapest they’ll ever be simply because nobody outside the organization and minor league baseball enthusiasts know most of these names yet. Here's a rough rule of thumb worth keeping in mind: the higher the signing bonus, the more attention collectors tend to pay, and that logic really kicks in once a bonus crosses $750,000. If a front office was willing to bet that kind of money on a teenager's upside, it's a fair question why a collector wouldn't take the same signal seriously.
Dawvris Brito signed for $1.2 million as the headliner of the 2026 international class, a shortstop with quick-twitch athleticism and triple-digit exit velocities already, and if there is a speculative play, I’d be playing in Brito’s camp. Garielvin Silverio signed for $1.4 million as a physical, left-handed-hitting corner outfielder with raw power, but is likely limited to a corner outfield spot due to lack of speed and athleticism.
Louis Andujar is the wild card of the group, and exactly the kind of story that makes chasing a bargain fun. Boston signed him for just $20,000 out of the Dominican Republic, a number so modest he barely registered outside the organization. He quietly hit .280 with a .974 OPS in the Dominican Summer League, then hit .410 with a 1.233 OPS in his stateside debut this year, good enough for FCL Hitter of the Week honors. If the $750,000 rule (that I made up completely) tells you who the industry believes in, Andujar is the opposite bet entirely, a near-free flier already outplaying his price tag.
The last name in this class comes with the best story attached. Enddy Azocar signed with Boston in January 2024 for just $40,000 out of Venezuela. He climbed all the way to the Red Sox's No. 5 prospect by this summer, hitting .286 with 18 home runs and 11 stolen bases in 85 games, right before Boston shipped him to Baltimore in the Rutschman trade. He hasn't missed a beat since, hitting .467 with a 1.238 OPS in his first 15 at-bats for High-A Frederick, and he's now the Orioles' No. 8 prospect. His 1st Bowman card will always have a Red Sox jersey, a snapshot of the last piece of a $40,000 bet Boston made and then dealt away for a franchise catcher.
Connelly Early carries that same wrinkle in a smaller way. Boston shipped him to the Nationals this July in the Curtis Mead deal, yet his Red RC in this release still has him in a Red Sox uniform. If you're a true Red Sox fan who likes owning a piece of the ones that got away, these are exactly those cards.
If you’re a top prospect hunter and have slept on Franklin Arias, this release gives you more chances to buy into his market, just not the way you'd expect. He doesn't get a 1st Bowman card this year (his 1st came last year), but he shows up with a prospect auto and two inserts as one of the sport's top prospects. If his original 1st Bowman wave passed you by, this is a more affordable way back into his market before he's an everyday big leaguer.
If you believe in Roman Anthony, the rest of this checklist is built for you. This year has been riddled with injury, a hand issue that kept him out for months. But zoom out. Boston signed this guy to an eight-year, $130 million extension back in August 2025, running through 2033 with a 2034 option and escalators that could push the value to $230 million.
That's a franchise betting on a 22-year-old being the face of this roster for the next decade, and Anthony's Red RC, Chrome Rookie Auto, Jumbo Chrome Autograph Relic, and Across the Seams autograph all reflect that same belief. If you're the kind of collector who buys into a player rather than a single season, the injury noise shouldn't scare you off so much as it should make this exact window the moment to buy in, before he's healthy and the price reflects it.
Every team in this release gets a shot at the future. Not every team has the history and memories that Red Sox fans have and names like Manny Ramirez, Roger Clemens, and Pedro Martínez in the same checklist should be like a slice of heaven. Ramirez lands in the Bowman Garbage Pail Kids (GPK) insert, a fitting nod to one of the most feared right-handed bats this franchise has ever run out. Clemens goes a step further with a base GPK card and an autograph version, and Pedro shows up in the Final Draft insert. None of these are prospect chases, and none will likely come cheap either, but they're closer to a tribute set than an investment. For a fanbase that grew up on these names, that's a fun thing to pull, regardless of cost.
Prices are always inflated in the first few weeks. Anthony's cards will likely cost the most, so waiting a month for the market to settle isn't unreasonable if you're patient. But Brito, Silverio, Azocar, and Andujar are cheap speculative buys worth grabbing now, and the Manny, Clemens, and Pedro pulls are worth paying up for if the fun of the rip matters more to you than the price tag.

item.content:encoded:
En casi cualquier parque de Grandes Ligas hay una historia dominicana. Puede estar en el lineup, en el bullpen o esperando su turno en el dugouts. La República Dominicana, una pequeña nación del Caribe con menos de 12 millones de habitantes, se convirtió en una de las mayores fábricas de talento del beisbol mundial.
Pedro Martínez, Vladimir Guerrero, Adrián Beltré y David Ortiz son parte de esa historia. También lo son Juan Soto, Fernando Tatis Jr. y Junior Caminero, una generación que mantiene a la isla como uno de los principales proveedores de peloteros para las Grandes Ligas. El año pasado, 144 jugadores dominicanos aparecieron en el Big Show, alrededor del 10 por ciento de todos los peloteros de la liga, de acuerdo con datos recopilados por ProPublica.
Detrás de cada firma existe una industria que comienza mucho antes de que un adolescente pueda ponerse la gorra de un equipo de Grandes Ligas. Entre 2012 y principios de 2026, las organizaciones de MLB pagaron 1,042 millones de dólares en bonos a prospectos dominicanos, de acuerdo con el análisis de ProPublica. Ese dinero alimenta a entrenadores, academias, intermediarios y prestamistas que conocen el sistema desde mucho antes de que el jugador llegue a un estadio de Grandes Ligas.
¿Cómo las mafias se aprovechan de los prospectos?
El problema comienza incluso antes de que exista una firma oficial. Los llamados preacuerdos permiten que equipos y prospectos pacten cantidades con años de anticipación, pese a que los jugadores internacionales no pueden firmar oficialmente hasta cumplir 16 años. Para las familias, el bono que algún día llegará puede convertirse desde mucho antes en una garantía para conseguir dinero inmediato.
Los entrenadores suelen recibir una parte importante del bono por haber formado al jugador, proporcionarle vivienda, alimentación y entrenamiento. ProPublica encontró casos en los que esa comisión llegó al 35 o 50 por ciento. Después aparecen los prestamistas, que entregan dinero a las familias utilizando como garantía una parte del futuro bono.
Una abogada que ha representado a jóvenes peloteros en disputas con entrenadores y prestamistas estimó que 80% de los bonos de Grandes Ligas pagados a prospectos dominicanos tienen algún préstamo asociado. Se calcula que hasta 500 millones de dólares de los 1,042 millones entregados entre 2012 y 2026 podrían terminar rápidamente en manos de entrenadores y prestamistas.
En ese mundo aparece Santo Caraballo. ProPublica lo describe como uno de los prestamistas más conocidos del beisbol dominicano. Su negocio consistía en entregar dinero a familias cuyos hijos tenían un preacuerdo con una organización de Grandes Ligas y cobrar después cantidades mucho mayores, utilizando el futuro bono como garantía. Caraballo defendió el modelo al explicar que el riesgo también estaba de su lado.
“Tú no sabes si se va a dar o no se va a dar, porque si el pelotero no firma, no cobras”, dijo en una entrevista a ProPublica.
Uno de los casos investigados es el de Belfi Rivera, quien a los 14 años llegó a un acuerdo verbal con los Diamondbacks por 1.8 millones de dólares. Cuando llegó el momento de cobrar, 630,000 dólares fueron para su entrenador, John Carmona, por una comisión equivalente al 35%. Más de 950,000 dólares terminaron en manos de Caraballo.
La familia de Belfi, de acuerdo con ProPublica, recibió inicialmente alrededor de 25,000 dólares. Los padres afirmaron que Caraballo les prestó ese dinero a cambio de recibir una cantidad mucho mayor cuando llegara el bono. La familia tenía poca experiencia financiera y, según el reportaje, ni siquiera recibió una copia del contrato que firmó.
Pero el nombre que hizo todavía más atractiva aquella relación fue el de David Ortiz.
Los padres de Belfi dijeron a ProPublica que Caraballo se presentó como la “mano derecha” de Ortiz. La reputación de Big Papi, una de las figuras más reconocidas de la historia reciente del beisbol dominicano, ayudó a generar confianza en una familia que estaba entrando por primera vez a un mundo en el que se manejaban cientos de miles de dólares.
Después, según los padres, Caraballo les habló de la posibilidad de invertir el dinero que todavía recibirían de los Diamondbacks en un negocio relacionado con él y Ortiz.
“Yo me puse contento porque ya mi muchacho va a tener una gente que le puede dar un consejo”, contó Eduardo Rivera a ProPublica.
La relación entre Ortiz y Caraballo no era una invención. Registros corporativos de Florida muestran que en 2021 ambos estuvieron vinculados con Big Papi Sports Group, una empresa que fue disuelta al año siguiente. Ortiz reconoció ante ProPublica que había invertido millones de dólares en el negocio de beisbol de Caraballo, aunque no precisó cuánto dinero ni identificó la empresa.
Ortiz aseguró que su relación empresarial con Caraballo estaba limitada a préstamos para entrenadores y que no trabajaba directamente con los padres de los prospectos porque recuperar ese dinero resultaba complicado. Sin embargo, ProPublica encontró un documento judicial en el que aparece el nombre de Ortiz en un contrato firmado con los padres de un jugador de 13 años.
El acuerdo establecía que Ortiz y Caraballo proporcionarían al menor alimentación, vivienda, estudios, entrenamiento, ropa, suplementos y oportunidades para ser observado por scouts. A cambio, recibirían 35% de su eventual bono de firma.
El jugador nunca firmó con una organización de Grandes Ligas y la demanda relacionada con el acuerdo fue desechada por cuestiones procesales. El documento, sin embargo, muestra que al menos en un caso el nombre de Ortiz sí apareció directamente en un contrato relacionado con un menor y con el futuro bono de un prospecto.
La investigación también documentó que Caraballo utilizaba la relación con Ortiz como parte de su capital de confianza. Padres, entrenadores y abogados consultados por ProPublica dijeron que el prestamista mencionaba al al Miembro del Salón de la Fama durante sus negocios.
Ortiz, por su parte, rechazó haber autorizado ese uso de su nombre.
“Yo nunca autoricé a Santo Caraballo a usar mi nombre o mi reputación para ganar la confianza de jóvenes peloteros o sus familias, para promover préstamos o inversiones, o para representar transacciones financieras como si fueran personalmente respaldadas por mí”, cito el reportaje por medio de un documento compartido por el abogado de Ortiz.
“Yo nunca participaría a sabiendas en ninguna operación que tenga la intención de tomar ventaja de un joven jugador o su familia”, extendió la cita.
Ortiz dijo además que comenzó a alejarse de Caraballo después de observar conductas que consideró inapropiadas. Según su declaración, la relación empresarial “comenzó a llegar a su fin” hace más de 18 meses y la relación personal terminó aproximadamente entre un año y medio y dos años antes de sus declaraciones a ProPublica.
La investigación, sin embargo, encontró una imagen que complica esa cronología. En septiembre de 2025, Ortiz y Caraballo viajaron juntos en un avión privado rumbo a Puerto Rico para asistir a un concierto de Bad Bunny.
La batalla de Ortiz en la disputa laboral de 2022
En 2022, MLB y el Sindicato de Jugadores negociaban un nuevo contrato colectivo y uno de los puntos más importantes era la posibilidad de establecer un draft internacional. La propuesta habría eliminado los preacuerdos que permiten a equipos y jugadores pactar cantidades antes de la edad oficial para firmar.
MLB defendía el draft como una manera de terminar con ese sistema. El sindicato se oponía porque consideraba que limitaría la capacidad de los prospectos para elegir equipo y eliminaría la competencia entre organizaciones que ayuda a elevar los bonos.
Ortiz intervino públicamente en favor de rechazar el draft. En un mensaje de voz dirigido a jugadores y entrenadores dominicanos, pidió organizar una campaña de oposición.
“Si permitimos que el draft suceda aquí en la República Dominicana, hasta sus tataranietos, y todos los demás, se verán afectados por él”, dijo Ortiz, según el audio obtenido por ProPublica. “Si dejamos que nos impongan eso aquí, estaremos en graves problemas”.
El draft no fue incluido finalmente en el acuerdo entre MLB y el sindicato.
Cuando ProPublica preguntó directamente a Ortiz si su oposición estaba relacionada con sus intereses empresariales junto a Caraballo, el exjugador no respondió y terminó la llamada.
Posteriormente, a través de su abogado, Ortiz negó que existiera una motivación económica detrás de su postura.
“Mi oposición a la propuesta de la liga nunca estuvo motivada por intereses personales”, señaló.
Según el comunicado, su postura estaba basada en sus opiniones sobre el desarrollo de los peloteros dominicanos y en el impacto que, a su juicio, tendría un draft internacional sobre el beisbol en el país.
El reportaje de ProPublica no establece que Ortiz haya cometido personalmente fraude o usura, ni que haya cobrado directamente los préstamos de los jóvenes. Documenta una relación empresarial y personal con Caraballo, un prestamista que obtuvo importantes cantidades de dinero de bonos de prospectos dominicanos.
